t.2.37.1: As long as the dust raised by him as he departed could still be seen, so long the foremost of the Ikṣvākus did not withdraw his eyes.
t.2.37.2: As long as the king could see his beloved and supremely righteous son, so long he seemed to rise taller upon the earth, straining for the sight of his son.
t.2.37.3: When the king could no longer see even the dust raised by Rāma, then, stricken and despondent, he fell down upon the surface of the earth.
t.2.37.4: The lady Kausalyā went to his right arm, and Kaikeyī, who held Bharata dear, went to his left side.
t.2.37.5: The king, endowed with prudence, righteousness and humility, his senses deeply troubled, looked at Kaikeyī and spoke to her.
t.2.37.6: Kaikeyī, do not touch my limbs, you woman of wicked conduct! For I do not wish to see you; you are neither my wife nor my kinswoman.
t.2.37.7: Those who depend on you, I am not theirs, nor are they mine. Since you are devoted to gain alone and have cast off dharma, I cast you off.
t.2.37.8: That I took your hand, and that I led you around the sacred fire, all of that I renounce, in this world and in the next.
t.2.37.9: If Bharata should be pleased at having obtained this imperishable kingdom, then whatever he may offer me for his father's sake, let that offering never reach me.
t.2.37.10: Then Queen Kausalyā, worn down by grief, raised up that lord of men, who was covered with dust, and turned back.
t.2.37.11: As one who has wilfully slain a brāhmaṇa, or as one who has touched fire with his hand, the righteous-souled king was consumed with remorse as he thought of his son become an ascetic.
t.2.37.12: As the king, turning back again and again, sank down in the tracks of the chariot, his form no longer shone brightly, like that of the sun when it is seized by eclipse.
t.2.37.13: Afflicted with grief, he lamented, remembering his beloved son. Then, knowing that his son had reached the edge of the city, he spoke.
t.2.37.15: Surely today he will lie down somewhere, sheltering at the foot of a tree, with a log of wood or else a stone placed beneath his head for a pillow.
t.2.37.14: The tracks of the excellent horses that carry that son of mine are seen upon the road, but that great-souled one himself is not seen.
t.2.37.17: Surely the men who roam the forest will see the long-armed Rāma, lord of the world, rising and going forth like one who has no protector.
t.2.37.16: And he will rise from the ground, wretched and covered in dust, sighing deeply, like a bull elephant rising from the watering place of the she-elephants.
t.2.37.18: Have your desire fulfilled, Kaikeyī; as a widow, rule the kingdom. For I cannot bear to live without that tiger among men.
t.2.37.19: Lamenting thus, the king, surrounded by a throng of people, entered the finest of cities like a man who, having taken the funeral bath, enters a house of ill omen.
t.2.37.20: He beheld the city with its squares and the ends of its houses deserted, its shops and shrines closed, its people weary, weak and stricken with grief, and its great highways not much thronged.
t.2.37.21: Having looked upon that whole city, the king, thinking only of Rāma and lamenting, entered his palace like the sun entering a cloud.
t.2.37.22: The house, bereft of Rāma, of Vaidehī and of Lakṣmaṇa, seemed like a great lake lying unstirred after Suparṇa has carried off its serpent.
t.2.37.23: "Let them quickly take me to the house of Kausalyā, Rāma's mother!" As the king spoke thus, the doorkeepers led him there.
t.2.37.24: Then, when he had entered Kausalyā's dwelling there, even after he had climbed onto his bed, his mind remained troubled and agitated.
t.2.37.25: And seeing that, the mighty great king raised his arm and cried out in a loud voice, "Alas, Rāghava, you are abandoning me!"
t.2.37.26: Ah, happy indeed will those best of men live at that time, who, embracing Rāma, will see him returned again!
t.2.37.27: I cannot see you, Kausalyā; touch me gently with your hand. My sight, which has followed Rāma, does not return even now.
t.2.37.28: Seeing the king upon his bed, thinking only of Rāma, the queen sat down close beside him and, looking deeply afflicted and sighing heavily, lamented grievously.
